title: How to Build a Retirement Plan If You Are Self-Employed With No Pension
description: The DIY pension: Solo 401(k)s and defined benefit plans.
content:
Self-employment offers freedom, but no safety net. You don't have a corporate pension, a 401(k) match, or subsidized health insurance. You are the CEO and the HR department. To retire securely, you must build your own 'Synthetic Pension' using the powerful tools available to business owners. The US tax code actually allows the self-employed to save *more* in tax-advantaged accounts than employees, provided you set up the right structures.

Key Takeaways

  • Solo 401(k): The best account for solopreneurs. Contribute up to $69,000 (2025) annually by maximizing both employee and employer sides. It beats the SEP IRA for most due to catch-up contributions.
  • Defined Benefit Plan: For high earners ($300k+), you can set up a personal pension plan that allows you to contribute $100k-$200k+ per year tax-deductible.
  • Business Sale is a Bonus: Do not count on selling your business to fund retirement. Treat the sale as a 'Lottery Ticket'. Fund your retirement accounts as if the business will be worth $0.
  • Tax Diversification: Use the Roth Solo 401(k) option to build tax-free wealth. Don't lock everything in pre-tax accounts.

Why It Matters (US Context)

As a self-employed person, you pay 15.3% SE Tax. Contributions to a Traditional Solo 401(k) reduce your *Income Tax*, but not the SE Tax. However, structuring as an S-Corp can help optimize the SE tax burden.

The Contribution Ladder

How to save $69,000+ per year.

Level 1: Employee Contribution

You can put in $23,000 (100% of income up to limit).
Note: This is the same limit as a W-2 worker.

Level 2: Employer Profit Sharing

Your business can contribute 20% of net profit (or 25% of W-2 salary if S-Corp).
Example: Net Profit $150,000. Employer contribution = ~$30,000.
Total: $53,000.

Level 3: Cash Balance Plan (Advanced)

If you are older (50+) and earn high income, you can layer a 'Defined Benefit Plan' on top. This allows contributions of $100k-$250k/year tax-deferred. It requires an actuary and fees, but saves massive taxes.

Business Exit Planning

  1. Automate Weekly: Don't wait for end-of-year profit. Set a weekly transfer of $500 to your Solo 401(k). Treat it like a payroll expense.
  2. Diversify: Don't reinvest 100% of profits into the business. Pull cash OUT. If your business fails, you need a separate nest egg in the S&P 500.
  3. The 'Rent' Strategy: If your business requires real estate, buy the building personally and rent it to the business. This creates a passive income stream (rent) for retirement even if you sell the operations.
  4. Health Insurance: Remember that premiums are tax-deductible for the self-employed. Use an HSA to build a tax-free medical fund.

Frequently Asked Questions

SEP IRA vs Solo 401k?

Solo 401(k) is usually better because it allows the $23k employee contribution even on lower income, plus catch-up contributions at 50, plus Roth options.

Do I need an actuary?

Only for a Defined Benefit plan. For a Solo 401(k), you can open it for free at Fidelity/Schwab with zero admin fees.

Can I borrow from it?

Solo 401(k) allows loans ($50k max). SEP IRAs do not. Another win for the Solo 401(k).
